URL: https://www.independent.co.uk/news/uk/politics/budget-john-healey-early-election-burnham-b3072960.html
The Independent — datePublished and dateModified both 2026-10-25T16:13:52Z = 16:13 GMT Sun 25 Oct. Retrieved by curl at 17:35 GMT.

HEADLINE SENSE: opposition parties and City institutions are preparing for an early election off the back of a "boring Budget".

ON THE RECORD — THE ONLY NAMED POLITICAL QUOTE IN THE PIECE
Andrew Griffith, shadow chancellor: "The Conservatives will be going through the Budget with a fine-toothed comb to make sure the facts see the light of day."

ON THE RECORD — NAMED CITY SOURCES
James Smith, ING economist, at a pre-Budget briefing in London, says an early election is "under priced": "Everything in UK politics at the moment seems to point in that direction. Burnham said back in August that this is a 10-year project. Currently, it's a three-year project." / "Frankly, a lot of these bold ambitions [from Burnham] are the sort of things you do on day one of a five-year term. So people are finding it very difficult to square that whole agenda with frankly quite a boring budget." / "These policies we're hearing about - bus fares and the VAT off energy bills - are eye-catching stuff that don't really cost a lot of money. It's the sort of thing you do if you're going to do an early election." On the delayed spending review: "It's the sort of thing you do after an election. I think that's why there's growing talk about whether you get an election next spring or summer ahead of that." And the counterweight: "I think markets probably wouldn't like an early election because I think there's a growing recognition that the UK actually looks quite good on fiscal policy. An early election will certainly be a catalyst for markets to think: 'Well, how do these big pledges get funded, is it going to be loose of fiscal rules?'"
Robert Salter, director at Blick Rothenberg: "One of the challenges facing the government from a fiscal policy is the commitment in the Labour Party's last election manifesto not to raise income taxes, NICs (national insurance contributions) or VAT during this Parliament. In this regard, it is worth remembering that income tax, NICs and VAT are the 'big three' taxes from a government tax receipts perspective and hence it is easy to see that the commitment in this area - even if not legally binding - restricts the freedom of the prime minister and chancellor from a tax policy perspective."

UNNAMED — DO NOT LEAD ON ANY OF THIS
"A source close to Kemi Badenoch", "One Tory source", "other City sources", "The Independent understands". The early-election framing, the "possibly in May or even earlier" timing, the claim that Badenoch's inner circle believes an early election is "highly likely", and the claim that candidates are being put in place in target seats are all unattributed.

EXPECTATIONS, NOT ANNOUNCEMENTS — all flagged by the Independent as expectation or understanding, none confirmed by the Treasury
Bank levy: "expected to hit banks with a levy increasing the tax on their profits from 3 per cent to as much as 8 per cent".
Capital gains tax: Healey "is understood to have turned down demands from cabinet colleagues for a hike".
Manifesto: Healey and Burnham "have insisted they will stick to Sir Keir Starmer's election manifesto promise not to raise income tax, VAT or employee national insurance contributions".
Also expected: more help with energy bills for low-income households; measures to bring down fuel duty; money for Burnham's plan to end rough sleeping.
Public sector pay: Healey "appears to be on course for a showdown with the trade unions... by not fully funding public sector pay rises and forcing departments to find the money from within their own budgets".
Debt measure: the Tories "have already raised questions about whether the chancellor will use the Public Sector Net Financial Liabilities (PSNFL) measurement, which is £365bn lower than Public Sector Net Debt (PSND), because it includes theoretical government assets, such as the student loans book."
ING's house view: "a boring budget, steady as she goes".
